lineage_context.teaching_goal: Use the local Linum flower-and-fruit plan—5 free petals, 5 stamens, 5 styles and a many-part capsule—as the family door, then contrast Malpighiaceae's clawed petals/oil-gland architecture.

project_scope.note: All five project-pool taxa are Linum. This lesson is intentionally built around the local genus rather than pretending one narrow key covers all global Linaceae.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: LOOK HERE FIRST: inspect one open Linum flower for five petals and FIVE FERTILE STAMENS (pollen-bearing anthers). The superior ovary has five carpels and five styles that may be free or joined nearly to their tips. Inspect ripe fruit for FIVE original locules; optional false septa may create ten apparent compartments. Capsules may open in FIVE OR TEN segments depending on species. Do not assume ten valves or five separate styles.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Local Linum are annual or perennial herbs with simple narrow leaves that may be alternate, opposite or whorled low on the stem; stipules are absent or gland-like.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Local Linum flowers usually have five sepals, five petals, five fertile stamens, and a superior five-carpellate ovary. Five styles can be free or connate. Staminodes (tiny sterile stamens) number zero or five in the genus, but are ABSENT in L. berlandieri, L. rigidum, L. hudsonioides and L. imbricatum according to Flora of North America. The ovary contains ovules; styles do not. Petals may fall early.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Dry capsule from five original carpels/locules, commonly with two ovules per locule. False septa may partially or nearly completely subdivide chambers; capsules open into five or ten segments depending on species. L. berlandieri, L. rigidum, L. hudsonioides and L. imbricatum have five two-seeded opening segments in Flora of North America. Never conflate original locules, false septa and dehiscence segments.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Count fertile anthers, not staminodes. Look for five carpels and the capsule; styles may be joined. Simple narrow leaves support identification but lower leaves can be opposite or whorled. Cistaceae commonly has many stamens, Geraniaceae beaked fruits, Oxalidaceae often ten stamens/compound leaves, and Malpighiaceae clawed petals/sepal glands.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: five fertile anthers vs joined styles → superior ovary → five primary locules vs optional false septa → five-or-ten fruit segments → species leaf/bract edges and family look-alikes
visual_lesson.intro: Count the five fertile pollen-bearing stamens and distinguish them from pollen-receiving styles. The styles are not necessarily free, and a five-carpellate capsule need not split into ten segments. Fruit sections and same-scale comparisons beat flower color.

comparisons.title: Linaceae vs Malpighiaceae
comparisons.rule: Both are Malpighiales with 5-part flowers, but local Linum is radial with ordinary free petals and five styles; Malpighiaceae commonly has opposite leaves, conspicuously clawed petals, often 10 stamens and sepal oil glands.

comparisons.title: Linaceae vs Geraniaceae
comparisons.rule: Both can be 5-merous herbs. Geraniaceae commonly forms a beaked schizocarp; local Linum forms a dry many-part capsule without the geranium beak.

comparisons.title: Linaceae vs Cistaceae
comparisons.rule: Both may have five free petals, but Cistaceae commonly has MANY stamens; local Linum has five fertile stamens. Inspect flower centers and fruit.

comparisons.title: Linaceae vs Oxalidaceae
comparisons.rule: Oxalis commonly has ten stamens and compound leaves, versus five fertile stamens and narrow simple leaves in local Linum. Confirm fruit before deciding.

visual_lesson.caveat: Global Linaceae is broader than Linum. This learner deliberately keys the project's one-genus pool.

genera.fast_cue: Five fertile stamens, five carpels, styles sometimes joined, capsule opening in five or ten segments; five project species.
